findings.source_passage: An instinct toward his future glory had led him, some months before, to the small Lutheran College of St. Olaf’s in southern Minnesota...
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning “An instinct toward his future glory…” (after the fairy’s-wing sentence)
findings.why_it_matters: This whole St. Olaf’s episode is the clearest evidence of Gatsby’s first abortive grab at self-betterment; critics routinely cite the “drums of his destiny” irony. Dropping it flattens the arc of self-invention.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the complete St. Olaf’s paragraph, including the janitor job and two-week walk-out, preserving Fitzgerald’s diction.

findings.source_passage: I remember the portrait of him up in Gatsby’s bedroom, a grey, florid man with a hard, empty face—the pioneer debauchee...
findings.source_locator: portrait paragraph immediately after Cody’s death
findings.why_it_matters: Nick’s acid sketch of Dan Cody and the champagne-in-the-hair anecdote are quintessential narrator voice and explain Gatsby’s own teetotal habit; cutting them removes character shading and Nick’s satiric tone.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the portrait description and liquor anecdote verbatim or with minimal trimming.

findings.source_passage: “Anything I hate is to get my head stuck in a pool,” mumbled Miss Baedeker… (full drunken-table exchange with Doc Civet)
findings.source_locator: tipsy supper-table sequence, between Daisy’s bad time and the movie-director vignette
findings.why_it_matters: The slapstick dialogue is a set-piece of West Egg excess and rounds out the party’s shift from glamour to grotesque; losing it thins Fitzgerald’s social satire.
findings.suggested_fix: Reinstate the Miss Baedeker / Doc Civet dialogue in concise form that preserves the drunken repartee and pool joke.

summary: Three voice- and interpretation-critical passages (St. Olaf’s, Cody portrait, drunken Miss Baedeker scene) are missing; restore them.
